title: Pastes or Mixtures
summary: The various pastes or mixtures are used as the base for sweet and savoury items in bakery. There are five basic pastes: (a) short crust paste, (b) flaky paste, (c) puff paste, (d) choux paste and (e) Danish paste. In confectionery the word pastry has a broader meaning and is synonymous with paste.

Do: work in a cool place with cool hands; sift the flour and salt after measuring (it incorporates air and lightens the pastry); use cold water and a round bladed knife for mixing; work quickly and handle the pastry as little and as lightly as possible; use lemon juice while making puff or flaky pastry (it strengthens the gluten and gives a lighter, crisper pastry); chill the pastry for 15-30 minutes after making (makes rolling easier and even); roll lightly and evenly with short strokes, always away from yourself; use very little flour for rolling; use a fairly hot oven (the high temperature makes the starch grains burst and absorb the fat, and creates steam that makes the pastry light); keep the work area and yourself clean. Do not: use tap or warm water; use too much water (the pastry becomes hard); over work the pastry; roll off the edge of the pastry (the air gets pressed out).
## Short crust, flaky and puff pastry

Short means friable or easily breakable; short crust paste is a mixture of flour, fat, sugar, baking powder and water, milk or egg. Flaky and puff pastry both need strong flour with good quality gluten, salt for taste, lemon juice as an acidic medium that strengthens the gluten, fat for layers and cold water to keep the dough temperature low so that the fat does not melt. Differences: puff pastry has fat and flour in the ratio 1:1, all the fat is folded in at one rolling, the layers are more and there are four empty rollings; flaky pastry has 3/4 of fat to every kilogram of flour, the fat is divided into three parts and folded in three rollings, the layers are fewer and there is only one empty rolling. A book fold divides the rectangle into four parts: the two outer parts are folded over the inner two and the pastry is folded again from the centre, giving four layers. The dough is rested for about half an hour covered with a moist duster and chilled in the freezer between rollings so that the fat stays firm. Products: vegetable patties, mushroom vol-au-vent, khara biscuits and cheese straws. Faults: too few layers (insufficient resting and chilling, heavy rolling or warm fat), fat running out (low baking temperature or poor flour), hard and tough pastries (too much water, over-kneading, baking in a cool oven), pastry unevenly risen (fat not evenly mixed, incorrect rolling or folding, not rested).

Choux paste is made by the boiled paste method: fat and water are boiled together and all the flour is added at once and cooked; the eggs are added only after the mixture has cooled, otherwise the egg proteins will coagulate. Gluten and albumin form a network that traps steam, so the products are very light with big hollow spaces. Steps: put butter and water in a thick bottomed degchi and bring to boil; add sieved flour all at one time, mixing vigorously; cook on slow fire until the mixture leaves the sides of the pan; cool to room temperature; add eggs one by one, mixing well; beat until firm enough to pipe. Eclairs are piped in finger shapes and baked at 210 C for 20-25 minutes, then another 10 minutes with the oven door open to prevent shrinking; profiteroles are small roundels and cream puffs are piped rosettes. Faults: pastry too thin (flour and liquid not cooked enough, mixture not beaten enough), too thick (liquid boiled for too long), close and solid texture (not beaten enough or oven too hot or too cool). Danish paste is made from a yeast dough enriched with layers of butter and is explained with yeast goods.

tf: Cheese straws are made from short crust paste.
False. They are made from puff (or flaky) pastry.
Lemon juice may be added while making puff pastry.
All the fat in puff paste is folded in one rolling.
When dough is over rolled, the product becomes hard.
Puff and flaky pastes always give different products.
False. The products that can be made are the same with a slight variation in texture.
The amount of fat used in flaky paste is more than that in puff paste.
False. Puff paste has more fat (1:1) than flaky paste (3/4:1).
Warm or tap water should be used for mixing pastry.
Eclairs shrink in size if they are removed too quickly from the oven.
True. The oven door is opened for another 10 minutes of baking to prevent shrinking.
sa: Give any five suggestions for preparing a good paste.

(i) Work in a cool place and keep your hands cool. (ii) Sift the flour and salt to incorporate air. (iii) Use cold water and do not use too much. (iv) Handle the pastry as little and as lightly as possible. (v) Chill the pastry for 15-30 minutes after making and bake it in a fairly hot oven.
Mention the steps of making choux paste.

(i) Put butter and water in a thick bottomed degchi and bring to boil. (ii) Add sieved flour all at one time, mixing vigorously. (iii) Cook on slow fire until the mixture leaves the sides of the pan. (iv) Cool to room temperature and add eggs one by one, mixing nicely. (v) Beat until firm enough to pipe and use as required.
Name the basic 5 pastes made in bakery.
(i) Short crust paste. (ii) Flaky paste. (iii) Puff paste. (iv) Choux paste. (v) Danish paste.
Differentiate between flaky pastry and puff pastry.

(i) Puff pastry has fat and flour in the ratio 1:1; flaky pastry has 3/4 fat to every kilogram of flour. (ii) In puff pastry all the fat is folded in at one rolling; in flaky pastry it is divided into three parts and folded in three rollings. (iii) Puff pastry has more layers; flaky pastry has fewer. (iv) Puff pastry has four empty rollings; flaky pastry has only one empty rolling.
Why do we chill puff or flaky paste between different rollings? State the common faults of these pastries.

(i) Chilling keeps the fat firm so that it does not melt or break through the dough layers. (ii) It relaxes the gluten and makes rolling easier. (iii) Faults: too few layers due to insufficient resting and chilling or warm fat. (iv) Fat running out during baking due to a low baking temperature. (v) Hard and tough pastry due to too much water, over-kneading or a cool oven.
